title: CIC 2 Task 2
reading_title: Campus Café to Launch 24-Hour Study Lounge
question_text: The woman expresses her opinion about the student union's plan to convert the café into a 24-hour study lounge. State her opinion and explain the reasons she gives for holding that opinion.
reading_body: The student union has announced that the campus café will soon be converted into a 24-hour study lounge during exam weeks. The café will close food service at 9 p.m., but remain open overnight as a quiet, monitored space for students who prefer to study late. The university believes this change will benefit students who struggle to find quiet study areas in the evenings, especially during finals. Extra seating and charging stations will also be added.

title: CIC 3 Task 2
question_text: The woman expresses her opinion about the university’s digital textbook policy. State her opinion and explain the reasons she gives for holding that opinion.
reading_body: Beginning next semester, all 100- and 200-level courses will require digital textbooks purchased through the university’s online portal. This change is being made for two reasons. First, bulk licenses negotiated with publishers will lower average costs for students and prevent out-of-stock delays that often occur at the start of the term. Second, digital texts provide academic features—search, built-in practice activities, instant updates, and accessibility tools such as screen readers and adjustable text—that support diverse learning needs. Print copies for these courses will not be stocked at the campus bookstore.

title: CIC 4 Task 2

listening_script.speaker: Woman
listening_script.line: Did you see the gym is switching to reservations at night?

listening_script.speaker: Man
listening_script.line: Yeah, and I actually support it. The line for treadmills after 6 is ridiculous. With time slots you know when you’ll get a machine.

listening_script.speaker: Woman
listening_script.line: But won’t the app just be another hassle?

listening_script.speaker: Man
listening_script.line: Not really. Their point about idle gaps is real. People step off to chat and machines sit empty while others wait. If the system releases no-shows after five minutes, the next person can hop on instead of guessing who’s “saving” a machine.

listening_script.speaker: Woman
listening_script.line: I still like being spontaneous, you know? I want to just walk in and run.

listening_script.speaker: Man
listening_script.line: You still can before 5 or after 9. Peak hours are the problem. And a 30-minute limit is fair—most workouts don’t need more than that for cardio. It spreads access so more students get a turn.

listening_script.speaker: Woman
listening_script.line: What if your class ends late and all the slots are gone?

listening_script.speaker: Man
listening_script.line: Then you can book earlier in the day, or use a different machine. The whole point is to replace a random line with a predictable schedule. That’s better than standing around for twenty minutes.

listening_script.speaker: Woman
listening_script.line: OK, I guess it addresses the two big issues—lines and wasted time on idle machines.

listening_script.speaker: Man
listening_script.line: Exactly. It’s a small change that makes peak hours actually usable.

question_text: The man expresses his opinion about the gym reservation plan. State his opinion and explain the reasons he gives for holding that opinion.
reading_body: Beginning next semester, the fitness center will require reservations for treadmills, bikes, and ellipticals during peak hours (5–9 p.m.). This change is being made for two reasons. First, recent observations show long lines at peak times, with some students waiting more than 20 minutes; timed reservations will reduce queuing and make access more predictable. Second, staff noted idle machines between informal rotations; 30-minute slots with a five-minute no-show release will increase equipment usage and reduce gaps. Walk-ins will remain available outside peak hours. Strength equipment and the track are not affected by this policy. Questions may be directed to the front desk.

title: CIC 5 Task 2

listening_script.speaker: Woman
listening_script.line: So we’re getting automated waitlists for enrollment on courses. Thoughts?

listening_script.speaker: Man
listening_script.line: Honestly, I’m against it as it's been described. They say it’s "fair," but a straight time stamp ignores priority cases—like seniors who need the class to graduate, or majors who need the course for their study plan.

listening_script.speaker: Woman
listening_script.line: The email volume is a mess, though. Automation would help.

listening_script.speaker: Man
listening_script.line: Sure, cut emails, but not by removing judgment. Right now instructors can look at context—graduation plans, prerequisites, even schedule conflicts. A blind queue can’t do that. You could be first in line but not ready for the lab, and then you block someone who is.

listening_script.speaker: Woman
listening_script.line: They could add rules—like priority for majors or seniors.

listening_script.speaker: Man
listening_script.line: Exactly, and until they build those rules in, the "fair placement" claim is weak. Also, that confirmation window worries me. If you’re in class or on a bus when the alert hits, you could lose the seat in an hour and have to start over.

listening_script.speaker: Woman
listening_script.line: So you want fewer emails, but smarter sorting.

listening_script.speaker: Man
listening_script.line: Right—use automation to assist decisions, not replace them. Include priority categories and a reasonable confirmation time. Then it would actually be fair and efficient.

question_text: The man expresses his opinion about the automated waitlist plan. State his opinion and explain the reasons he gives for holding that opinion.
reading_body: Starting next term, full courses will use an automated waitlist in the registration system. This change will have several benfits.Time-stamped queues provide fair placement and reduce informal requests, ensuring students are added in a clear, consistent order when seats open. In addition, an automated process will reduce email back-and-forth with instructors and staff, who currently handle hundreds of add requests manually. Students may join multiple waitlists and will receive a notification if a seat becomes available; they must confirm within a limited window or the seat will pass to the next student in line.

title: CIC 6 Task 2

listening_script.speaker: Woman
listening_script.line: Did you see they’re making double-sided printed the default for all college printers?

listening_script.speaker: Man
listening_script.line: Sure, and I think it's a great idea. The lab printers run out of paper every afternoon. If the default cuts usage, that means fewer lines.

listening_script.speaker: Woman
listening_script.line: But some assignments need single-sided—like lab reports you have to scan, or... pages with diagrams.

listening_script.speaker: Man
listening_script.line: You can still switch it in the settings. The announcement says single-sided is allowed; it’s just not the default. Most readings print fine double-sided, and it helps with the second reason they gave: fewer jams. When the trays are stuffed with single-sided jobs, the queue gets backed up.

listening_script.speaker: Woman
listening_script.line: I’ve had prints come out mixed—some pages upside down.

listening_script.speaker: Man
listening_script.line: Yeah, but... that’s a settings issue. They should post a one-page guide next to each printer: “flip on long edge,” that kind of thing. It's a small fix.

listening_script.speaker: Woman
listening_script.line: mmm. I’m mainly worried about speed between classes.

listening_script.speaker: Man
listening_script.line: Well, that's exactly why this helps! If we use half the paper, staff spend less time refilling trays and clearing jams. This means faster turnover and shorter waits. And... you still keep the option to go single-sided when you need it.

question_text: The woman expresses her opinion about the printing policy. State her opinion and explain the reasons she gives for holding that opinion.
reading_body: Beginning next semester, all college printers will default to double-sided output. Switching the default will reduce paper use, lowering costs and the number of restocks during peak times. Furthermore, double-sided jobs lead to fewer paper jams in high-volume queues, which shortens wait times and keeps printers available. Single-sided printing will remain possible: users may change the setting at the print dialog for specific jobs. The per-semester page allowance is unchanged, but students are encouraged to save pages by previewing documents and avoiding unnecessary reprints.

title: CIC 7 Task 2

listening_script.speaker: Man
listening_script.line: Did you see the new rule about uploading a draft before the final paper is due?

listening_script.speaker: Woman
listening_script.line: Yeah, and I support it. The whole point is to get feedback while there’s still time to fix things. The tool catches basic problems—unclear sentences, citation formatting—so you turn in a cleaner paper. It also flags missing references early, which helps students avoid last-minute integrity issues. I’d rather find those warnings a day before the deadline than after the professor grades it.

listening_script.speaker: Man
listening_script.line: It still feels like an extra step. Some of us work late or commute—forcing a draft a day early adds pressure.

listening_script.speaker: Woman
listening_script.line: You can still submit the final on the real due date. The draft upload is just a checkpoint so you don’t leave everything to the last night. Honestly, that structure helps. You upload a rough version, skim the report, and make targeted fixes. It ends up saving time because TAs don’t mark the same basic errors over and over.

listening_script.speaker: Man
listening_script.line: I’m also not convinced the software understands writing in different majors. And what about privacy?

listening_script.speaker: Woman
listening_script.line: No tool is perfect, but it’s useful for fundamentals—grammar, citations, simple clarity. You keep control: you decide which suggestions to accept. As for privacy, instructors only see that you ran the check; they don’t grade the report itself. Our papers already live in the learning system—this just adds an early scan to prevent careless mistakes.

listening_script.speaker: Man
listening_script.line: So you think the benefits outweigh the hassle?

listening_script.speaker: Woman
listening_script.line: Definitely. It gives everyone a free round of feedback and reduces accidental citation problems before they count. If you plan ahead a little, it makes final submission smoother and less stressful.

question_text: The woman expresses her opinion about the draft-check requirement. State her opinion and explain the reasons she gives for holding that opinion.
reading_body: Beginning next semester, students will be required to upload a draft of any major paper to the university’s draft-check system at least one day before the final due date. The system provides free automated feedback on clarity, grammar, and citation format so students can improve their work before grading. Secondly, early similarity checks will reduce last-minute academic integrity problems by flagging missing citations in time to fix them. Instructors will receive a brief confirmation that a draft was checked; grades will not be based on the report. Students who miss the draft deadline may still submit the assignment, but a late-draft note will appear.

title: CIC 8 Task 2

listening_script.speaker: Woman
listening_script.line: Did you see they want us to scan a code at the start of lecture?

listening_script.speaker: Man
listening_script.line: Yeah, and I’m not a fan. The whole idea depends on phones working perfectly—signal, battery, the app loading—and if any of that fails, you look “absent” even when you’re sitting there.

listening_script.speaker: Woman
listening_script.line: But they’re trying to fix messy paper sheets and start class faster.

listening_script.speaker: Man
listening_script.line: I get that, but this trades one problem for another. In a big hall, the projector freezes or the code doesn’t load, and now we’re wasting time troubleshooting. Plus there’s the privacy angle. I don’t love tying my location to an app every class, even if they say it’s just attendance.

listening_script.speaker: Woman
listening_script.line: The notice said you can check in with the TA if your phone isn’t working.

listening_script.speaker: Man
listening_script.line: Which becomes a line after class. And it’s not just tech issues. People will scan and leave unless there’s a quiz or activity tied to the day. If the real goal is a fair record, there are simpler options—card swipes at the door, or a one-question slip collected once a week that shows you were actually engaged.

listening_script.speaker: Woman
listening_script.line: So you’d skip the QR code altogether?

listening_script.speaker: Man
listening_script.line: Yeah. Keep attendance simple and reliable—no phones required—and use quick in-class checks to prove participation. That meets both goals without new headaches.

question_text: The man expresses his opinion about the QR scan-in policy. State his opinion and explain the reasons he gives for holding that opinion.
reading_body: To improve record-keeping in large lecture courses, the university will pilot a quick scan-in at the start of class. A QR code will appear on the screen during the first ten minutes, and students will check in with the campus app; late arrivals should speak with the TA. Electronic check-ins create consistent, time-stamped attendance lists, which helps ensure participation points are recorded fairly. As well as this, replacing paper sign-in sheets will reduce interruptions caused by passing clipboards and collecting signatures, so lectures can begin on time. The scan records attendance for the specific class only; students without a device may confirm with the TA after class.
